title: 22. Interview: Server-Sent Events (SSE)
summary: Interview Q&A for Server-Sent Events (SSE) — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Server-Sent Events (SSE) interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What are Server-Sent Events, and how do they differ from WebSockets?
**Answer:** SSE is an HTTP-based unidirectional push protocol: the browser opens a single long-lived GET to a `text/event-stream` endpoint, the server keeps the response open and writes `data:`-prefixed events as they occur, and the browser's native `EventSource` API receives them. WebSockets are a full-duplex bidirectional protocol that upgrades an HTTP connection to a frame-based wire protocol. Key differences: (1) **Direction** — SSE is server-to-client only; the client must use a separate POST to send data back; WebSockets are bidirectional on one connection. (2) **Protocol** — SSE is plain HTTP (works through any HTTP infrastructure, cacheable in some setups, simple to debug with curl); WebSockets upgrade to a custom binary protocol (requires Upgrade-aware proxies, sticky sessions for scaling). (3) **Browser API** — SSE has the native `EventSource` with built-in auto-reconnect and `Last-Event-ID` cursor; WebSockets require manual reconnection and resume logic. (4) **Data format** — SSE is text-only (UTF-8); WebSockets support text and binary. (5) **Overhead** — SSE has one set of HTTP headers for the connection's lifetime; WebSockets have a 2-14 byte frame header per message. (6) **Use case** — SSE for server-to-client push (live feeds, notifications, ChatGPT token streaming, GitHub Actions logs); WebSockets for bidirectional (chat, multiplayer, collaborative editing). ChatGPT, Twitter live feed, and GitHub Actions logs all use SSE; WhatsApp, Slack, Discord use WebSockets.
**Visual:**
```
SSE:         client --GET /stream--> server (held open)
             client <--data: event1--
             client <--data: event2--
             (one-way, native EventSource, auto-reconnect w/ Last-Event-ID)

WebSocket:   client --Upgrade--> server --101--> (bidirectional)
             client <--frame--> server (text/binary, any time)
             (two-way, manual reconnect, sticky sessions to scale)
```

### Q2. What is the `text/event-stream` wire format?
**Answer:** The wire format is a stream of UTF-8 text where each event is a set of lines terminated by a blank line (`\n\n`). Each line is a `field: value` pair where field is one of `id`, `event`, `data`, or `retry`. A simple event is `data: hello\n\n` — the browser fires `onmessage` with `e.data = "hello"`. A named event adds an `event:` line: `event: alert\ndata: price drop\n\n` — the browser fires `addEventListener("alert", ...)` with `e.data = "price drop"`. An event with an id adds `id: 42\n` — the browser stores 42 as the last event ID and includes it as `Last-Event-ID: 42` on reconnect. The `retry: 5000` field tells the browser to wait 5000 ms before reconnecting after a drop. Multi-line data uses multiple `data:` lines that the browser joins with `\n`: `data: line one\ndata: line two\n\n` becomes `e.data = "line one\ntline two"`. Lines starting with `:` are comments (ignored by the browser) and are used as keep-alive heartbeats (`: ping\n\n`). The format is intentionally minimal — it's parseable line-by-line without a state machine, and humans can read it with `curl`. This simplicity is SSE's main advantage over WebSockets for one-way push.
**Visual:**
```
text/event-stream wire format:

data: hello\n\n                              -> onmessage, e.data="hello"

event: alert\ndata: price drop\n\n           -> onalert,    e.data="price drop"

id: 42\ndata: msg with id\n\n                -> onmessage, e.lastEventId=42
                                              (browser sends Last-Event-ID: 42
                                               on reconnect)

data: line one\ndata: line two\n\n           -> onmessage, e.data="line one\ntline two"

retry: 5000\n\n                              -> browser waits 5s before reconnect

: ping\n\n                                   -> comment, ignored (keep-alive)
```

### Q3. How does `Last-Event-ID` resume work?
**Answer:** When the server includes an `id:` field in an event, the browser stores that id internally as `EventSource.lastEventId`. If the connection drops (network glitch, server restart, proxy timeout), the browser automatically reconnects after the `retry:` interval (default 3 seconds) by issuing a fresh GET to the same URL with the `Last-Event-ID: <id>` HTTP header set to the last received event id. The server reads this header, queries its event store for events with id greater than the last-received, and replays them in order before resuming live push. This is exactly the cursor-based replay pattern used in Kafka consumer offsets (Phase 6) and WhatsApp's message delivery. The browser handles reconnection and cursor management natively — the application code just sets `id:` on each event and the server implements "events with id > N" lookup. Without `Last-Event-ID`, a dropped connection mid-stream would silently lose any events that happened during the disconnect window. With it, those events are replayed on reconnect. Caveat: the server must persist events (not just hold them in memory on the parked response) for the replay to work across server restarts; a typical design is a ring buffer of the last N events per stream in Redis, with N chosen to cover the maximum expected reconnect window (say 1000 events or 5 minutes, whichever is smaller). ChatGPT, Twitter live feed, and GitHub Actions logs all use `id:`-tagged events for resume.
**Visual:**
```
client receives: id:1, id:2, id:3 (drops at id:3)
client reconnects: GET /stream
  Last-Event-ID: 3
server: SELECT * FROM events WHERE id > 3 ORDER BY id
  -> replays id:4, id:5 (missed during disconnect)
  -> then live push id:6, id:7 ...
client sees: 4, 5, 6, 7 (no loss, no duplicate)
```

### Q4. What is the browser connection limit, and how does HTTP/2 fix it for SSE?
**Answer:** Browsers historically limited HTTP/1.1 to 6 concurrent connections per origin (Chrome, Firefox, Safari all follow this; it's a long-standing convention to prevent any single site from exhausting the client's resources). If you open 6 SSE streams on one origin, you've used all 6 connections — any other HTTP request (XHR, image load, fetch) is blocked until an SSE stream closes. This was a real problem for SSE adoption in the HTTP/1.1 era. HTTP/2 fixes this: HTTP/2 multiplexes many logical streams over a single TCP connection, so the 6-connection limit doesn't apply — you can have dozens of SSE streams on one origin without blocking other requests. All modern browsers support HTTP/2 (since ~2015), and most CDNs and reverse proxies (Cloudflare, AWS ALB, NGINX) support HTTP/2 by default. The practical advice: (1) Use HTTP/2 end-to-end (browser → CDN → origin) if you're using SSE; (2) if you can't, limit yourself to one SSE stream per origin and use event names (`event: alert`, `event: tick`) to multiplex logical channels over one stream; (3) for many streams across many origins, use a wildcard subdomain (`s1.example.com`, `s2.example.com`) to get more connection slots — but this is a hack and HTTP/2 is the right answer. The 6-connection limit is essentially a non-issue in 2024 with HTTP/2, but it's worth knowing for older systems.
**Visual:**
```
HTTP/1.1: 6 connections per origin max
  SSE stream 1  |----open----|
  SSE stream 2  |----open----|
  SSE stream 3  |----open----|
  SSE stream 4  |----open----|
  SSE stream 5  |----open----|
  SSE stream 6  |----open----|
  XHR /fetch    BLOCKED until an SSE closes

HTTP/2: one TCP connection, many multiplexed streams
  SSE stream 1  |--|----|--|------|----|
  SSE stream 2  |--|----|------|----|---|
  SSE stream 3  |--|------|----|----|---|
  XHR /fetch    |--|----|--|----|------|   (no blocking)
  (all share one TCP connection, no limit)
```

### Q5. Why must you disable proxy buffering for SSE, and how?
**Answer:** Many reverse proxies and CDNs buffer the response body until it reaches a certain size (typically 4-8 KB) or the connection closes, then forward it as a single chunk. This is great for static content (saves TCP packets) but catastrophic for SSE: if the proxy buffers, the browser doesn't see events until the buffer fills (which may take minutes for small events) or the connection closes (which defeats the purpose of SSE). The result is that the SSE stream appears "stuck" — no events arrive for a long time, then a burst arrives at once. To fix: (1) **NGINX** — set `proxy_buffering off;` in the location block for the SSE endpoint, OR set the response header `X-Accel-Buffering: no` which NGINX respects per-response. (2) **Apache** — `mod_proxy` with `SetEnv proxy-sendchunked 1` and disable `ProxyPass ... flushpackets=off` (set to `on`). (3) **Node.js Express** — set `res.setHeader("Content-Type", "text/event-stream")` and call `res.flushHeaders()` after writing the status line; with HTTP/2, use `res.flush()` after each event. (4) **Python** — in a WSGI server, use a streaming response (Flask `stream_with_context`, Django `StreamingHttpResponse`); in asyncio, `yield` from a generator with `await response.drain()`. (5) **CDN** — Cloudflare and AWS CloudFront buffer by default; configure caching=off and use the `Cache-Control: no-cache` header. (6) **Send periodic heartbeats** — a comment line (`: ping\n\n`) every 15 seconds keeps the connection alive through idle-connection timeouts even if buffering is enabled. The diagnostic is simple: `curl -N https://your-endpoint/stream` (the `-N` disables curl's buffering); if you see events immediately, your server is fine and the problem is upstream proxies.
**Visual:**
```
without buffering disabled:
  server writes: data: e1\n\n
                 data: e2\n\n
                 data: e3\n\n  (3 small events)
  proxy buffers (waits for 4KB)
  browser sees: (nothing... nothing... nothing...)
                 data: e1\ndata: e2\ndata: e3\n\n  (burst after 30s)

with buffering disabled (X-Accel-Buffering: no or proxy_buffering off):
  server writes: data: e1\n\n
  browser sees: data: e1\n\n  (instant)
  server writes: data: e2\n\n
  browser sees: data: e2\n\n  (instant)

+ heartbeat every 15s:
  : ping\n\n  (comment, ignored by browser, keeps proxy alive)
```

### Q6. How would you scale SSE horizontally to millions of connections?
**Answer:** SSE shares the "many idle stateful connections" characteristic with WebSockets, so the scaling recipe is similar but with some SSE-specific twists. (1) **Async server** — required; one OS thread per parked SSE response is unaffordable at scale. Use Node.js, Python asyncio, Go, Java Netty, or Erlang. Each parked connection costs a few KB of memory. (2) **Sticky load balancing** — not strictly required for SSE (the connection is stateless from the LB's perspective: a fresh GET can go to any backend), but required if the server holds per-user state (subscriptions, replay buffer). Use a session cookie or hash of user_id for stickiness. (3) **Pub/sub fan-out** — when a backend service wants to push to user X, it publishes to a Redis/Kafka/NATS channel that every SSE server subscribes to; the server holding X's connection delivers. (4) **Event store for replay** — persist recent events (last N per stream) in Redis or ScyllaDB so a reconnecting client with `Last-Event-ID` can be served by any backend, not just the one that had the original connection. (5) **Connection draining** — when a server is being decommissioned, the LB stops sending new connections; existing connections continue until the client disconnects or the server sends a `retry: 0` event to force a quick reconnect (the browser reconnects immediately to a different backend). (6) **Per-connection memory cap** — bound the replay buffer per connection; if a slow client falls behind, drop old events and send a "you missed N events" notification. (7) **HTTP/2** — enables many SSE streams per TCP connection, reducing kernel socket pressure. Twitter, LinkedIn, and ChatGPT all run SSE at scale with this pattern.
**Visual:**
```
1M SSE clients
   |
  HTTP/2 load balancer (sticky by session cookie)
   |
  20 SSE gateway nodes (50k conns each, async)
   |  per-node: in-memory user_id -> response stream map
   |  per-node: replay buffer (last 1000 events per stream)
   |
  Redis pub/sub (channel per user, per topic)
   |
  backend services (publish events)

reconnect: client sends Last-Event-ID
  any backend can serve (reads replay buffer from Redis)
  -> sticky not strictly required, but reduces cache misses
```

### Q7. Why does ChatGPT use SSE for token streaming instead of WebSockets?
**Answer:** ChatGPT's token streaming is the canonical SSE use case. The reasons SSE beats WebSockets here: (1) **Unidirectional** — the client sends one prompt (via POST), the server streams tokens back (via SSE); there's no need for the client to push anything during generation. WebSockets' bidirectional capability is wasted. (2) **Works through fetch** — `EventSource` cannot POST (it only GETs), so ChatGPT uses a `fetch` with a streaming reader (`response.body.getReader()`) that consumes the SSE-formatted chunks manually. This is a common pattern for "SSE-shaped" streams that need a POST body. (3) **Standard HTTP infra** — load balancers, CDNs, auth proxies, rate limiters all understand HTTP request-response; SSE rides on this without modification. WebSockets require Upgrade-aware infrastructure and sticky sessions. (4) **Per-token backpressure** — the server writes one event per token (or per token batch) and flushes; the client reads at its own pace; HTTP's flow control handles backpressure. (5) **No connection state** — each completion request is a fresh SSE stream that closes when the response is done; no need to maintain a long-lived WebSocket per user. (6) **Reconnect not needed** — if the stream drops mid-generation, the client simply re-issues the completion request (the server may resume from a checkpoint, but typically the user just gets a partial answer and re-submits). (7) **Simpler client** — `fetch` + reader is roughly 30 lines of JavaScript; WebSocket client with reconnection and resume would be 100+. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, and Mistral all use SSE for their token streaming APIs.
**Visual:**
```
client: POST /v1/chat/completions  (body: {messages, stream:true})
  Accept: text/event-stream

server: 200 OK
        Content-Type: text/event-stream
        data: {"choices":[{"delta":{"content":"Hello"}}]}\n\n
        data: {"choices":[{"delta":{"content":" world"}}]}\n\n
        data: {"choices":[{"delta":{"content":"!"}}]}\n\n
        data: [DONE]\n\n
        (connection closes)

client reads chunks via fetch().body.getReader(), parses SSE,
appends each delta to displayed text -> user sees "Hello world!"
forming word-by-word in real time
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You are building a live-updating dashboard (stock prices, weather, system metrics). SSE, WebSocket, or long polling?
**Answer:** **SSE is the right answer** for a live-updating dashboard. Reasoning: (1) **Direction** — dashboards are pure server-to-client; the server pushes updates, the client just receives and renders. WebSockets' bidirectional capability is wasted; long polling's per-cycle overhead is wasteful. (2) **Browser API** — `EventSource` is native, auto-reconnects with `Last-Event-ID`, and handles backpressure. Long polling requires a manual XHR loop with custom reconnection. (3) **Multiple channels** — use named events (`event: stock`, `event: weather`, `event: metric`) to multiplex logical streams over one SSE connection, avoiding the browser's per-origin connection limit. (4) **Resume on reconnect** — `Last-Event-ID` lets the server replay missed updates after a network drop, so a brief disconnection doesn't lose data. (5) **Simplicity** — the server is a streaming HTTP endpoint (one handler per stream), the client is 30 lines of JS, and there's no sticky-session or pub-sub complexity until you scale past one server. (6) **HTTP/2 multiplexing** — multiple SSE streams (one per dashboard widget) share one TCP connection, reducing overhead. (7) **Fallback** — for users behind proxies that block SSE, fall back to long polling (the same endpoint can serve both; if the client sends `Accept: text/event-stream`, return SSE; otherwise, return a JSON snapshot and the client polls). Bloomberg's web terminal, Datadog's live dashboards, and GitHub's live Actions logs all use SSE for this exact pattern. WebSockets would be overkill; long polling would be a step backward.
**Visual:**
```
dashboard client opens ONE SSE stream:
  GET /dashboard/stream  Accept: text/event-stream

server pushes named events on one connection:
  event: stock\ndata: {"ACME": 142.50}\n\n
  event: weather\ndata: {"temp": 72}\n\n
  event: metric\ndata: {"cpu": 0.45}\n\n
  event: stock\ndata: {"ACME": 142.55}\n\n
  ...

client: es.addEventListener("stock", ...) -> update stock widget
        es.addEventListener("weather", ...) -> update weather widget
        es.addEventListener("metric", ...) -> update metric widget

one connection, multiple logical channels, auto-reconnect w/ Last-Event-ID
```

### Q2. Your SSE endpoint works in Chrome but events arrive in bursts in Safari. Diagnose.
**Answer:** Burst-y delivery in Safari (or any specific browser) where Chrome works fine points to a buffering issue at the application or proxy layer that one browser tolerates and the other doesn't. Hypotheses: (1) **Server-side buffering** — the server framework is buffering the response and flushing in chunks. Chrome and Safari have different receive-buffer thresholds; Chrome may flush on each `\n\n`, Safari may wait for a larger buffer. Fix: explicitly flush after each event (in Python `wfile.flush()`, in Node.js `res.flush()`, in Go `Flusher.Flush()`). (2) **NGINX proxy_buffering** — NGINX buffers responses by default; if `proxy_buffering off;` isn't set on the SSE location, NGINX accumulates events until its buffer fills, then forwards a burst. The `X-Accel-Buffering: no` header should disable this per-response; verify it's being sent. (3) **Compression** — if the response is gzip-compressed, the compressor buffers until it has enough data to compress efficiently, then flushes a chunk. Disable compression for SSE endpoints (`Content-Encoding: identity` or turn off `gzip` for `text/event-stream`). (4) **CDN buffering** — Cloudflare's "Rocket Loader" or "Auto Minify" can interfere; set `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-transform` and consider disabling caching on the SSE endpoint. (5) **HTTP/2 frame buffering** — some HTTP/2 implementations coalesce small frames; setting `Cache-Control: no-cache` and sending periodic heartbeats (`: ping\n\n` every 5s) forces a flush. (6) **Diagnostic** — `curl -N https://your-endpoint/stream` from the Safari user's network; if curl sees bursts, the problem is server/proxy; if curl sees events immediately, the problem is Safari-specific (rare). The fix is almost always "explicitly flush after each event, disable buffering and compression, send heartbeats".
**Visual:**
```
symptom: Chrome shows events as they arrive (instant)
         Safari shows events in bursts every ~10s

causes (in order of likelihood):
  1. server not flushing after each event        -> add wfile.flush()
  2. NGINX proxy_buffering on                     -> X-Accel-Buffering: no
  3. gzip compression buffering                   -> disable for text/event-stream
  4. CDN buffering (Cloudflare Auto Minify)       -> Cache-Control: no-transform
  5. HTTP/2 frame coalescing                      -> send : heartbeat every 5s
  6. Safari-specific (rare)                       -> check with curl -N

diagnostic: curl -N https://endpoint/stream
  if curl bursts: server/proxy issue
  if curl is instant: Safari issue (very rare)
```

### Q3. You need to stream a 10 GB log file to a browser in real time as it's written. SSE or WebSockets?
**Answer:** **SSE is the right answer** for streaming a log file. Reasoning: (1) **Direction** — log streaming is pure server-to-client; the client subscribes and receives lines as they're written. No client-to-server traffic needed. (2) **Native API** — `EventSource` handles reconnection and resume via `Last-Event-ID`; if the connection drops, the browser reconnects and the server resumes from the last-seen byte offset (or line number). (3) **Text format** — logs are text, which matches SSE's text-only constraint perfectly. WebSockets would add binary capability that's unused. (4) **Simplicity** — the server is a generator that tails the file and yields `data: <line>\n\n`; the client is `es.onmessage = e => appendLine(e.data)`. (5) **Backpressure** — HTTP flow control handles slow clients; if the browser can't keep up, the server's write blocks (or, in async frameworks, the await on `response.drain()` blocks). (6) **GitHub Actions precedent** — GitHub's CI log streaming uses exactly this pattern: the build runs, logs are written to a file, an SSE endpoint tails the file and streams lines to the browser. (7) **Resume after reconnect** — if the user's connection drops mid-build, `Last-Event-ID` (set to the byte offset or line number) lets the server replay missed lines on reconnect. WebSockets would require custom reconnection logic and would still need a separate "send me logs since X" message protocol. The only reason to prefer WebSockets here would be if the client also needed to send commands (e.g., "pause tail", "filter by level") over the same connection — but even then, a separate POST is simpler.
**Visual:**
```
server endpoint: GET /logs/stream?file=app.log
  - open file, seek to Last-Event-ID (byte offset) if provided
  - tail the file, yield each new line as SSE event:
      id: <byte_offset>
      data: <log_line>
      \n\n
  - flush after each event
  - send : ping\n\n every 15s to keep alive

client:
  es = new EventSource("/logs/stream?file=app.log")
  es.onmessage = e => appendLine(e.data)
  // on reconnect, browser sends Last-Event-ID: <byte_offset>
  // server seeks to that offset and resumes tailing
```

### Q4. Your SSE server holds 100k connections but restarts every deploy, causing all clients to reconnect simultaneously. How do you avoid the thundering herd?
**Answer:** A simultaneous restart of an SSE server triggers 100k browsers to reconnect within seconds (the default `retry:` is 3 seconds), causing a connection spike that can overwhelm the new server or the load balancer. Mitigations: (1) **Staggered restart** — rolling deploy: restart one server at a time, wait for connections to drain before moving to the next. With 10 servers, restarting one at a time spreads the reconnect load across 10 deploy windows. (2) **Send `retry:` directive before disconnect** — when the server is about to shut down, send each client `retry: <random 1-30 seconds>\n\n` followed by closing the connection. The browser waits the random interval before reconnecting, spreading the load across 30 seconds. (3) **Connection draining** — the load balancer stops sending new connections to the draining server; existing connections continue until the client disconnects or the server forces a close with a `retry:` directive. (4) **Client-side jitter** — the client adds its own random jitter (1-10 seconds) on reconnect, even if the server didn't send `retry:`. This is a defense-in-depth measure. (5) **Backoff at the LB** — if the new server sees connection rate exceed a threshold, it returns 503 with `Retry-After` to slow the reconnect wave. (6) **Long retry default** — set the server's default `retry:` to 5-10 seconds instead of the browser's 3-second default; this gives the deploy more time to complete before reconnects start. (7) **Replay buffer** — the server persists the last N events in Redis so reconnecting clients can resume without missing data, eliminating the urgency of immediate reconnect. Slack, Discord, and Twitter all do staggered deploys with `retry:` directives for exactly this reason.
**Visual:**
```
naive: server restarts, 100k clients reconnect in 3s window
  -> LB / new server overwhelmed

fix 1: staggered restart (rolling deploy)
  restart server 1 of 10 -> 10k reconnects
  wait 60s
  restart server 2 of 10 -> 10k reconnects
  ... (10 windows, 10k each)

fix 2: server sends retry: <random 1-30s> before close
  client 1: retry: 5s   -> reconnects at t+5s
  client 2: retry: 12s  -> reconnects at t+12s
  client 3: retry: 22s  -> reconnects at t+22s
  ... (spread over 30s)
```

### Q5. You are streaming ChatGPT-style tokens over SSE. The user clicks "Stop generating" mid-stream. How do you implement this?
**Answer:** The "stop generating" feature requires server-side cancellation of the in-progress generation, but SSE itself is server-to-client only — the client cannot send a "stop" message over the SSE stream. The recipe: (1) **Client-side abort** — the client calls `fetchController.abort()` on the `AbortController` used to issue the original POST request; this closes the SSE stream from the client side. The server's response stream gets a broken pipe / connection reset on its next write, which it should catch and clean up. (2) **Server-side cancellation** — the client also sends a separate POST to `/v1/chat/completions/cancel` with the completion ID (returned in the first SSE event or in the response headers); the server looks up the in-progress generation by ID and signals the model inference loop to stop. This is necessary because the SSE abort may take a TCP RTT to propagate, and the model may continue generating tokens (and consuming GPU) in the meantime. (3) **Cancellation propagation** — if the server is calling downstream model servers (e.g., a vLLM or TensorRT-LLM backend), it must propagate the cancellation via gRPC deadline/cancellation (Phase 2 Topic 12) or a shared cancellation channel. (4) **State preservation** — the client keeps the partial response it has received so far; when the user asks a follow-up, the partial response is included in the conversation history as if it were complete (with an indicator that it was cut short). (5) **Billing** — the server records how many tokens were generated before cancellation, for billing and metering. ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude, and Google Gemini all implement this pattern: client-side abort + server-side cancel endpoint + cancellation propagation to the inference backend.
**Visual:**
```
client: POST /v1/chat/completions  (stream=true)
  <- SSE stream starts, tokens flow: data: Hello\ndata: world\ndata: ...

user clicks "Stop":
  client: abortController.abort()         // closes SSE stream
  client: POST /v1/chat/cancel {id: ...}  // tell server to stop

server:
  - SSE write fails (broken pipe) -> catch, cleanup
  - cancel endpoint signals inference loop to stop
  - propagate cancellation to vLLM backend (gRPC cancel)
  - record partial tokens for billing

client keeps partial response "Hello world" in conversation history
```

### Q6. Your SSE endpoint is behind AWS CloudFront and clients see events delayed by 30+ seconds. Diagnose.
**Answer:** CloudFront buffers responses by default and is not SSE-aware out of the box — this is a classic SSE-behind-CDN problem. The 30+ second delay is the buffer filling up before CloudFront forwards the chunk. Fixes: (1) **Disable caching on the SSE path** — in CloudFront, set the cache behavior for `/stream*` to "CachingDisabled" and the origin protocol policy to "HTTPS-only" (CloudFront won't cache streaming responses). (2) **Disable response buffering** — CloudFront's default behavior buffers small responses; you must configure the distribution to forward responses as they arrive. As of 2024, CloudFront does support streaming responses for HTTP/2, but only if the origin sends `Cache-Control: no-cache` and `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`. (3) **Bypass CloudFront for SSE** — the simplest fix is to route SSE traffic directly to the origin (e.g., `sse.example.com` is a DNS record pointing to the ALB, not through CloudFront). ChatGPT and similar services often do this — the main site is behind CloudFront, but the SSE token-streaming endpoint is on a separate hostname that bypasses the CDN. (4) **Use a different CDN** — Cloudflare Workers and Fastly both have first-class SSE support with no buffering, because they were designed for edge compute with streaming responses. AWS CloudFront added streaming response support relatively recently and it's still finicky. (5) **Heartbeat** — send a `: ping\n\n` comment every 5 seconds; even if CloudFront is buffering, the heartbeat will eventually fill the buffer and force a flush, bounding the delay to one buffer-fill interval. (6) **Diagnostic** — `curl -N https://your-cdn-endpoint/stream` and time how long it takes to see the first event; if it's instant, CloudFront is fine and the problem is elsewhere; if it's 30s, CloudFront is buffering. The pragmatic answer is "bypass CloudFront for SSE endpoints" — it's the most reliable fix.
**Visual:**
```
client -> CloudFront -> origin (SSE server)

problem: CloudFront buffers response until 8KB or close
  server writes: data: e1\n\n  (20 bytes)
  CloudFront: buffering... (needs 8KB)
  server writes: data: e2\n\n  (20 bytes, total 40 bytes)
```

### Q7. You need to send binary data (images, audio chunks) to the browser in real time. SSE, WebSocket, or HTTP/2 streaming?
**Answer:** **WebSockets are the right answer** for binary real-time data. SSE is text-only (UTF-8) — binary data must be base64-encoded, which inflates size by 33% and adds CPU cost for encode/decode on both sides. For a few small images this is tolerable; for a stream of audio chunks at 100 KB/sec, the 33% overhead is 33 KB/sec of wasted bandwidth and noticeable CPU. WebSockets support binary frames natively (opcode 0x2), with no encoding overhead — the bytes go on the wire as-is. Reasoning: (1) **Native binary** — WebSocket binary frames carry raw bytes; SSE would require base64. (2) **Backpressure** — WebSockets have per-frame backpressure via TCP flow control; SSE has HTTP-level flow control which also works but is coarser. (3) **Bidirectional** — if the client also sends binary (e.g., microphone audio for real-time transcription), WebSockets handle it on the same connection; SSE would require a separate POST. (4) **Latency** — WebSockets have 2-14 byte frame overhead; SSE has 5-20 bytes of `data: ` prefix plus base64 expansion; for high-frequency small binary messages, WebSockets win. (5) **HTTP/2 streaming** — for very large binary downloads (video on demand), plain HTTP/2 with `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` is better than either — it's cacheable, resumable with `Range:` headers, and supported by every CDN. Decision tree: small text events → SSE; small to medium binary real-time → WebSocket; large binary download (non-real-time) → HTTP/2 chunked with Range; voice/video real-time → WebRTC (UDP-based, designed for low-latency audio/video). Discord voice uses WebRTC; ChatGPT token streaming uses SSE; YouTube video uses HTTP/2 chunked with Range.
**Visual:**
```
decision tree for binary to browser:
  small text events (logs, JSON, tokens)  -> SSE
  small/medium binary real-time (audio, images)
                                           -> WebSocket (binary frames)
  large binary download (video on demand) -> HTTP/2 chunked + Range
  real-time voice/video                    -> WebRTC (UDP, RTP, Opus)

SSE for binary: must base64 -> 33% size overhead + CPU cost
  example: 100KB audio chunk
    SSE:     133KB on wire (base64) + UTF-8 validate + JSON parse
    WebSocket: 100KB on wire (binary frame) + no encoding
```
